The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume Countable Choice and let $d\ge1$ be an integer. Work in
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$\langle u,v\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u\overline v$, linear in the first
variable, using the quotient and complex-function conventions of the linked
Euclidean $L^2$ definitions. Fix real scalars $m>0$, $\hbar>0$, and $q$.
Let $A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be real and
let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ satisfy
$V\ge-v_0$ almost everywhere for some finite $v_0\ge0$. Put
$\mathscr D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and, for $u\in\mathscr D$,
define
$$\Pi_j^A u=-i\hbar\,\partial_j u-qA_j u\qquad (1\le j\le d).$$
For $u,v\in\mathscr D$ define the sesquilinear form
$$q_{A,V}(u,v)=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\langle\Pi_j^A u,\Pi_j^A v\rangle+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)u(x)\overline{v(x)}\,dx,$$
and write $q_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}(u,u)$. Each integral is finite: the test
functions and their magnetic derivatives are bounded with compact support,
and $V$ is integrable on compact sets. The form is Hermitian, densely
defined, and bounded below by $-v_0\|u\|_2^2$.

For $\varepsilon_0>0$ define its shifted form norm by
$$\|u\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}^2=q_{A,V}[u]+(v_0+\varepsilon_0)\|u\|_2^2.$$
The form is **closable** when every sequence $(u_n)\subset\mathscr D$ with
$\|u_n\|_2\to0$ and
$\|u_n-u_m\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$ as $n,m\to\infty$ also satisfies
$\|u_n\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$. This condition is independent of the
choice of $\varepsilon_0>0$. When it holds, the **closed form closure** is the
completion of $\mathscr D$ in this norm, identified with its $L^2$ limits;
the corresponding closed form is denoted $\overline q_{A,V}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix
$\hbar>0$ and an integer $d\ge1$, and work in the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\overline g$ linear in the first
argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**Weak derivatives.** For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and
$j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, say that the $j$-th weak derivative of $f$ exists in
$L^2$ when there is a class $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,D_j\varphi=(-1)\int_{\mathbb R^d}g\,\varphi \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d),$$
where $D_j\varphi$ is the classical partial derivative and the pairing is
bilinear without conjugation ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).
Such a $g$ is unique as an $L^2$ class
([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]); write $D_jf:=g$.
The Sobolev space $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of classes
$f\in L^2$ for which $D_1f,\dots,D_df$ all exist in $L^2$, and
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of $f\in W^{1,2}$ with
$D_jf\in W^{1,2}$ for every $j$, with $D_jD_kf$ written for the iterated
derivative ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

**(a) Position operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(Q_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ x\mapsto x_jf(x)\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)\},\qquad (Q_jf)(x):=x_jf(x).$$
Thus $Q_jf$ is the class of the pointwise product with the $j$-th coordinate
function.

**(b) Momentum operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(P_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ D_jf\text{ exists in }L^2\},\qquad P_jf:=-i\hbar\,D_jf .$$

Both $Q_j$ and $P_j$ are densely defined $\mathbb C$-linear operators in
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$: for $Q_j$ the compactly supported smooth
classes lie in the domain because $x_j$ is bounded there, and for $P_j$ they
lie in the domain because their classical derivatives are weak derivatives in
$L^2$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

For density, the classes of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ are dense in
$W^{0,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ by
[[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]] and
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. Since these classes lie in each domain
as above, both operator domains are dense.

For a class
$f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ one has $Q_jf=x_jf$ and
$P_jf=-i\hbar\,\partial_jf$ pointwise. The self-adjointness of these operators
and their Fourier representation are proved in
the companion self-adjointness lemma on this page, not
asserted here; for $d=1$ the domain $D(P)$ of the single momentum operator
coincides with $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Fix $\varepsilon_0>0$ and put $W=V+v_0$. For every $u\in C_c^\infty$,
$$\|u\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}^2=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\|\Pi_j^A u\|_2^2+\|W^{1/2}u\|_2^2+\varepsilon_0\|u\|_2^2.$$
This identity shows that if $(u_n)$ is Cauchy in the shifted form norm,
then each sequence $(\Pi_j^A u_n)$ and $(W^{1/2}u_n)$ is Cauchy in $L^2$.

Suppose additionally that $\|u_n\|_2\to0$. Let $w_j$ be the $L^2$
limit of $\Pi_j^A u_n$. For any $\phi\in C_c^\infty$, symmetry [F2]
and Cauchy–Schwarz give
$$\langle w_j,\phi\rangle=\lim_n\langle\Pi_j^A u_n,\phi\rangle=\lim_n\langle u_n,\Pi_j^A\phi\rangle=0.$$
Density in [F1] implies $w_j=0$. If $w_0$ is the $L^2$ limit of
$W^{1/2}u_n$, then [F3] and Cauchy–Schwarz similarly give
$$\langle w_0,\phi\rangle=\lim_n\langle u_n,W^{1/2}\phi\rangle=0$$
for every test function $\phi$, so density gives $w_0=0$.

Every term on the right side of the norm identity in step 1.1 therefore
tends to zero, including $\varepsilon_0\|u_n\|_2^2$. Thus
$\|u_n\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$, which is exactly the closability
criterion in [[def-nrqmx-magnetic-form-data]]. The completion is densely
embedded in $L^2$ because it contains the dense core, and the criterion makes
that embedding injective; its form is closed by construction and retains the
lower bound $-v_0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\lambda_n$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ as defined in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and completed from Borel measure as in [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]. The product measure $\lambda_a\times\lambda_b$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and under $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$, $\lambda_{a+b}$ is its completion ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]). Write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a,\lambda_a)$ and $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b,\lambda_b)$, with $L^2$ understood as the almost-everywhere quotient of square-integrable measurable functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

$2\pi kn$ to the argument of sine and cosine. Each $e_k$ is continuous, hence
Borel, and satisfies

$$e_k(x)e_l(x)=e_{k+l}(x),\qquad |e_k(x)|=1,\qquad \overline{e_k(x)}=e_{-k}(x) ,$$

the last two by the cartesian form $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of
[[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]. In particular $e_0=1$ and every
$e_k$ is bounded and nonzero everywhere.

**Fourier coefficients.** Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), that is, a class
of Borel functions with $\int_{\mathbb T}|f|\,dm_{\mathbb T}<+\infty$. Define the
**Fourier coefficient** of $f$ at $k\in\mathbb Z$ by

$$\widehat f(k):=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)\exp(-2\pi ikx)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$

This is well defined: $|f\,e_{-k}|=|f|$ because $|e_{-k}|=1$, so
$f\,e_{-k}\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and its integral is finite; and the
integral depends only on the class of $f$, because it is unchanged when $f$ is
modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The characters
$(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]): they are
orthonormal and their closed linear span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axioms of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]).
Use the spaces of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]] and the
absolutely continuous representatives supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-intervals-weak-derivative-ac-representative]].

(a) *Bounded intervals.* Let $0<L<\infty$ and $u,v\in H^1(0,L)$. Then
$\int_0^Lu\,\overline{v'}=u^*(L)\overline{v^*(L)}-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}
-\int_0^Lu'\,\overline v .$

(b) *Endpoint-vanishing space.* $H^1_0(0,L)=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(0)=u^*(L)=0\}$,
with the traces $u^*(0),u^*(L)$ of the continuous representative.

(c) *Second-order identity.* For $u,v\in H^2(0,L)$,
$\int_0^L\bigl(u''\overline v-u\,\overline{v''}\bigr)
=\bigl[u'^*\overline{v^*}-u^*\overline{v'^*}\bigr]_0^L,$
where the bracket denotes
$u'^*(L)\overline{v^*(L)}-u^*(L)\overline{v'^*(L)}
-u'^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}+u^*(0)\overline{v'^*(0)}$.

(d) *Half-line and line.* If $u,v\in H^1(0,\infty)$, then
$\int_0^\infty u\overline{v'}=-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}-\int_0^\infty u'\overline v$, both integrals
being absolutely convergent. For $u,v\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ one instead has
$\int_{\mathbb R}u\overline{v'}=-\int_{\mathbb R}u'\overline v$,
with both integrals absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim:
Set $A_0=-\kappa\partial_\phi^2$ on $H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)$. In the
boundary coordinates $\Gamma_0f=(f(0),f(2\pi))$ and
$\Gamma_1f=(f'(0),-f'(2\pi))$, the unitary swap matrix in [F1] makes the
boundary equation equivalent to $f(0)=f(2\pi)$ and
$f'(0)=f'(2\pi)$: adding and subtracting its two scalar equations gives
these two equalities. Hence $-\partial_\phi^2$ is self-adjoint on this
domain, and multiplication by the positive real $\kappa$ shows that $A_0$
is self-adjoint. Let $P=-i\partial_\phi$.
Integration by parts [F5] and equality of the endpoint traces show that $P$ is
symmetric on $H^2_{\mathrm{per}}$. For $f=\sum_nc_ne_n$ in this domain,
integration by parts gives $\langle Pf,e_n\rangle=nc_n$ and
$\langle A_0f,e_n\rangle=\kappa n^2c_n$. Parseval for [F2] therefore
implies $\|Pf\|_2^2=\sum_n n^2|c_n|^2$ and
$\|A_0f\|_2^2=\kappa^2\sum_n n^4|c_n|^2$.

On $D(A_0)$ write
$T_\alpha=A_0+B_\alpha$ with
$B_\alpha=-2\kappa\alpha P+\kappa\alpha^2I$. This operator is symmetric
because $P$ is symmetric and $\alpha,\kappa$ are real. For every
$\varepsilon>0$ and integer $n$,
$|n|\le\varepsilon n^2+(4\varepsilon)^{-1}$; the coefficient identities
in step 1.1 and the triangle inequality give
$\|B_\alpha f\|_2\le a\|A_0f\|_2+b\|f\|_2$ with any prescribed $a>0$
after choosing $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small and then a finite $b$.
Applying [F3] with $a<1$ proves that $T_\alpha$ is self-adjoint on the
stated periodic domain.

Each $e_n$ lies in the periodic domain and direct differentiation gives
$T_\alpha e_n=\kappa(n-\alpha)^2e_n$. Completeness [F2] makes this the full
orthonormal eigenbasis. The associated spectral projections are therefore
the sums of the character projections whose eigenvalues lie in the chosen
Borel set, so every scalar spectral measure is supported on
$\{\kappa(n-\alpha)^2:n\in\mathbb Z\}$. This set has no finite accumulation
point because $\kappa>0$ and $|n-\alpha|\to\infty$. If $z$ is outside it,
$\inf_n|\lambda_n-z|>0$. For $f=\sum_nc_ne_n$, where
$c_n=\langle f,e_n\rangle$, the diagonal map
$R_zf=\sum_n c_n(\lambda_n-z)^{-1}e_n$ is bounded on $H$. Also
$\sup_n|\lambda_n/(\lambda_n-z)|<\infty$, so the domain characterization
in [F4] shows that $R_z$ maps into $D(T_\alpha)$. Coefficientwise,
$(T_\alpha-z)R_z=I$ and $R_z(T_\alpha-z)=I$ on $D(T_\alpha)$, so $z$ is
in the resolvent. If $z=\lambda_n$ then $e_n$ is a nonzero kernel vector.
Hence the spectrum is exactly the
displayed set and there is no continuous spectral measure.

Let $j\in\mathbb Z$ and $U_jf=e^{ij\phi}f$. It is unitary, preserves
the periodic $H^2$ domain, and
$(P-\alpha-j)U_jf=U_j(P-\alpha)f$ by differentiation; squaring gives
$T_{\alpha+j}U_j=U_jT_\alpha$. If a smooth periodic unit-modulus function
$u$ satisfies the displayed conjugacy, then $(P-\alpha)u=0$, or
$u'=i\alpha u$.
The solutions are $u(\phi)=c e^{i\alpha\phi}$ with $|c|=1$, which are
periodic exactly when $e^{2\pi i\alpha}=1$, equivalently $\alpha\in\mathbb Z$.
Conversely, for integral $\alpha$ this multiplier is single-valued and
periodic.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, $m,\hbar>0$, and real $q,B$
with $qB\ne0$. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ close the nonnegative form
$$q_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C).$$
Put $\omega_c=|qB|/m$,
$E_n=\hbar\omega_c(n+\tfrac12)$, and let $(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ be the
complete normalized eigenfunctions of the one-dimensional oscillator with
mass $m$, frequency $\omega_c$, and action constant $\hbar$ in its exact
self-adjoint oscillator realization. For
Schwartz $u$ define
$\mathcal F_yu(x,k)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-iky}u(x,y)\,dy$,
and use its unitary $L^2$ extension. Put $x_0(k)=\hbar k/(qB)$ and
$(Uu)(\xi,k)=\mathcal F_yu(\xi+x_0(k),k)$.
Then $U$ is unitary from $L^2(\mathbb R^2_{x,y})$ onto
$L^2(\mathbb R^2_{\xi,k})$. Writing
$$Uu(\xi,k)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(k)\psi_n(\xi),\qquad f_n\in L^2(\mathbb R_k),$$
the form closure domain and value are exactly
$$D(\overline q_B)=\left\{u:\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n\|f_n\|_{L^2(k)}^2<\infty\right\},\qquad \overline q_B[u]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n\|f_n\|_{L^2(k)}^2.$$
Thus the form is the diagonal oscillator form with an unrestricted $L^2(k)$
degeneracy factor; it asserts no finite-area state count.

Assume Countable Choice and let $d\ge1$ be an integer. Work in
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$\langle u,v\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u\overline v$, linear in the first
variable, using the quotient and complex-function conventions of the linked
Euclidean $L^2$ definitions. Fix real scalars $m>0$, $\hbar>0$, and $q$.
Let $A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be real and
let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ satisfy
$V\ge-v_0$ almost everywhere for some finite $v_0\ge0$. Put
$\mathscr D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and, for $u\in\mathscr D$,
define
$$\Pi_j^A u=-i\hbar\,\partial_j u-qA_j u\qquad (1\le j\le d).$$
For $u,v\in\mathscr D$ define the sesquilinear form
$$q_{A,V}(u,v)=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\langle\Pi_j^A u,\Pi_j^A v\rangle+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)u(x)\overline{v(x)}\,dx,$$
and write $q_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}(u,u)$. Each integral is finite: the test
functions and their magnetic derivatives are bounded with compact support,
and $V$ is integrable on compact sets. The form is Hermitian, densely
defined, and bounded below by $-v_0\|u\|_2^2$.

For $\varepsilon_0>0$ define its shifted form norm by
$$\|u\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}^2=q_{A,V}[u]+(v_0+\varepsilon_0)\|u\|_2^2.$$
The form is **closable** when every sequence $(u_n)\subset\mathscr D$ with
$\|u_n\|_2\to0$ and
$\|u_n-u_m\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$ as $n,m\to\infty$ also satisfies
$\|u_n\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$. This condition is independent of the
choice of $\varepsilon_0>0$. When it holds, the **closed form closure** is the
completion of $\mathscr D$ in this norm, identified with its $L^2$ limits;
the corresponding closed form is denoted $\overline q_{A,V}$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, $m,\hbar>0$, and real $q,B$
with $qB\ne0$. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ close the nonnegative form
$$q_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C).$$
Put $\omega_c=|qB|/m$,
$E_n=\hbar\omega_c(n+\tfrac12)$, and let $(\psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ be the
complete normalized eigenfunctions of the one-dimensional oscillator with
mass $m$, frequency $\omega_c$, and action constant $\hbar$ in its exact
self-adjoint oscillator realization. For
Schwartz $u$ define
$\mathcal F_yu(x,k)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-iky}u(x,y)\,dy$,
and use its unitary $L^2$ extension. Put $x_0(k)=\hbar k/(qB)$ and
$(Uu)(\xi,k)=\mathcal F_yu(\xi+x_0(k),k)$.
Then $U$ is unitary from $L^2(\mathbb R^2_{x,y})$ onto
$L^2(\mathbb R^2_{\xi,k})$. Writing
$$Uu(\xi,k)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(k)\psi_n(\xi),\qquad f_n\in L^2(\mathbb R_k),$$
the form closure domain and value are exactly
$$D(\overline q_B)=\left\{u:\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n\|f_n\|_{L^2(k)}^2<\infty\right\},\qquad \overline q_B[u]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n\|f_n\|_{L^2(k)}^2.$$
Thus the form is the diagonal oscillator form with an unrestricted $L^2(k)$
degeneracy factor; it asserts no finite-area state count.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\lambda_n$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ as defined in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and completed from Borel measure as in [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]. The product measure $\lambda_a\times\lambda_b$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and under $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$, $\lambda_{a+b}$ is its completion ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]). Write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a,\lambda_a)$ and $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b,\lambda_b)$, with $L^2$ understood as the almost-everywhere quotient of square-integrable measurable functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let $\beta$ be the standard flat function. The **standard smooth step function** is
$$ \sigma(t):=\frac{\beta(t)}{\beta(t)+\beta(1-t)}. $$
Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that

$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

First apply the unitary planar map from [F1] at each fixed $z$, then the
partial Fourier transform in $z$ from [F2]. On the dense product core both
maps are unitary; the Euclidean $L^2$ product identifications in [F2] extend
their composition uniquely to a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$. The inverse
uses the inverse Fourier transforms and the opposite translation, which is
measure preserving by [F3]. The coefficient map in the transverse variable
is unitary because $(\psi_n)$ is a complete orthonormal basis. Thus $U_3$ is
unitary onto the stated coefficient space.

Let $f=(f_n)$ have finite weighted norm and fix $\varepsilon>0$. Since
the defining nonnegative series converges, choose $N$ so the norm of its
tail over $n>N$ is below $\varepsilon/3$. For the finitely many indices
$n\le N$, the weighted integrals outside
$K_R=[-R,R]_{k_y}\times[-R,R]_{k_z}$ tend to zero as $R\to\infty$ by
dominated convergence, so choose one $R$ making their combined tail norm
below $\varepsilon/3$. Define
$$\eta_R(k_y,k_z)=\prod_{s\in\{k_y,k_z\}}\sigma(R+1-s)\sigma(R+1+s).$$
It equals one on $K_R$, is between zero and one, and has support in
$K_{R+1}$ by [F4]. For each $n\le N$, truncate $f_n$ to $K_R$ and
approximate that truncation in unweighted $L^2$ by
$\varphi_n\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ using [F4]. The function
$g_n=\eta_R\varphi_n$ is smooth and supported in $K_{R+1}$, and on that
box $E_n+ck_z^2\le E_n+c(R+1)^2$. Since $\eta_R=1$ on $K_R$ and
$0\le\eta_R\le1$, choose each of the finitely many $L^2$ errors small
enough that the weighted norm difference between $g_n$ and the truncation
has combined norm below $\varepsilon/3$. Set $g_n=0$ for $n>N$. The
triangle inequality then gives a finite family
$g_0,\ldots,g_N\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ within $\varepsilon$ of $f$
in the weighted coefficient norm.

For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, every $z$-slice
$u(\cdot,\cdot,z)$ is a planar test function. Apply the form identity in
[F1] on those slices and integrate in $z$ by Fubini. The $z$ derivative
commutes with the planar transform; after Fourier transformation in $z$,
Plancherel and the derivative identity in [F2] turn
$\|-i\hbar\partial_zu\|_2^2/(2m)$ into the multiplier $ck_z^2$. Tonelli
[F5] permits summing the nonnegative transverse energies and integrating in
$(k_y,k_z)$. Therefore
$$q^{(3)}_B[u]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}(E_n+ck_z^2)|f_n(k_y,k_z)|^2\,dk_y\,dk_z.$$
This makes the transformed core an isometric subspace of the stated weighted
coefficient space.

For the finite family from step 1.2 put
$G(\xi,k_y,k_z)=\sum_{n=0}^Ng_n(k_y,k_z)\psi_n(\xi)$. Its inverse is
$$v(x,y,z)=\frac1{2\pi}\sum_{n=0}^N\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{i(k_yy+k_zz)}g_n(k_y,k_z)\psi_n\!\left(x-\frac{\hbar k_y}{qB}\right)dk_y\,dk_z.$$
Each coefficient is smooth and compactly supported in $(k_y,k_z)$, and each
$\psi_n$ is a polynomial times a Gaussian by [F7]. Every derivative of the
integrand is smooth with compact wave-number support and has uniformly rapid
decay in $x$ because $k_y$ remains in a bounded set. Repeated integration
by parts in $k_y,k_z$ gives arbitrary polynomial decay in $y,z$; the same
estimates hold after any fixed $x,y,z$ derivatives. Thus $v$ is Schwartz.
Define
$$\chi_R(x,y,z)=\prod_{s\in\{x,y,z\}}\sigma(2-s/R)\sigma(2+s/R),$$
using the smooth step from [F4]. These cutoffs equal one on $[-R,R]^3$,
vanish outside $[-2R,2R]^3$, and satisfy $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. For
each covariant derivative,
$$\Pi_j(\chi_Rv)=\chi_R\Pi_jv-i\hbar(\partial_j\chi_R)v,$$
where $\Pi_x=-i\hbar\partial_x$, $\Pi_y=-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx$,
and $\Pi_z=-i\hbar\partial_z$. Dominated convergence [F8] sends
$(\chi_R-1)\Pi_jv$ and $(\chi_R-1)v$ to zero in $L^2$, while the added
term has norm at most $C\hbar\|v\|_2/R$. Hence $\chi_Rv$ approximates
$v$ in the form norm and belongs to the original compactly supported core.
Thus each finite smooth coefficient family from step 1.2 lies in the
transformed form closure.

Step 2.1 embeds the transformed core isometrically into the weighted
coefficient space. Because the form completion is complete and the weighted
target is complete by [F6], the isometric image of the completion is closed
in that target. Steps 1.2 and 2.2 show that a dense subspace of the entire
weighted space lies in the image, so the image is the whole target. This
identifies the completion and its quadratic form as stated.

Use SI units with mass $m>0$ in kilograms, charge $q\in\mathbb R$ in
coulombs, action constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, vector-potential
components $A_j$ in tesla-metres, and scalar potential-energy function $V$ in
joules. For each integer $d\ge1$, let $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$
be real and let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ be bounded
below. Adopt the general-dimensional minimal-coupling assignment whose core
form is
$$q_{A,V}[u]=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\|(-i\hbar\partial_j-qA_j)u\|_2^2+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V|u|^2,\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C).$$
Use its closed form closure and the unique self-adjoint representing
Hamiltonian. For dimensional form norms use the fixed reference energy
$E_0=1\,\mathrm J$: apply the closed-form representation to
$q_{A,V}/E_0$ and multiply the representing operator by $E_0$.

The magnetic-field notation is dimension-specific. In $d=2$, with coordinates
$(x,y)$ and $A=(A_x,A_y)$, define the scalar perpendicular field
$$B_\perp(x,y)=\partial_xA_y(x,y)-\partial_yA_x(x,y),$$
in teslas. Thus $A=(0,Bx)$ gives $B_\perp=B$ for a constant signed scalar
$B$. In $d=3$, for coordinates $(x,y,z)$ and $A=(A_x,A_y,A_z)$, define the
field vector $\mathbf B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ in teslas by
$$\mathbf B=(\partial_yA_z-\partial_zA_y,\ \partial_zA_x-\partial_xA_z,\ \partial_xA_y-\partial_yA_x)=\nabla\times A.$$
No magnetic-field object is assigned by this notation in $d=1$.

For an optional spin-half degree of freedom in three dimensions, define
$$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_j=\frac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_j.$$
For a core spinor $u=(u_1,u_2)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^2)$,
define the spin-independent form
$$q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}[u_1]+q_{A,V}[u_2].$$
For a declared dimensionless real coupling $g$, adopt the effective Pauli core

$$q^{\mathrm P}_{A,V,g}[u]=q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]-\frac{gq}{2m}\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(x)^*(S\cdot\mathbf B(x))u(x)\,dx,$$
where $u^*$ is conjugate transpose and
$(S\cdot\mathbf B)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^3S_jB_j(x)$ for the three-dimensional

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let
$S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ with angular coordinate $\phi$, and identify
$L^2(S^1;\mathbb C)$ with $L^2((0,2\pi),d\phi;\mathbb C)$; the omitted

For $f\in H^2(0,2\pi)$ use the continuous endpoint representatives of $f$ and $f'$, and denote their traces by $f^*(0),f^*(2\pi)$ and $(f')^*(0),(f')^*(2\pi)$. Define

derivations.claim:
On the circle, arclength is $s=R\phi$, so the tangential derivative is
$\partial_s=R^{-1}\partial_\phi$. The circulation of the constant tangential
potential is $\int_0^{2\pi}A_\phi R\,d\phi=\Phi$ by [A1]. Therefore the
covariant tangential momentum supplied by [F1] is
$$-i\hbar\partial_s-qA_\phi=\frac1R\left(-i\hbar\partial_\phi-\frac{q\Phi}{2\pi}\right).$$
Dividing its square by $2m$ gives the Hamiltonian in the Statement and the
dimensionless parameter $\alpha=q\Phi/(2\pi\hbar)$.

Put $\kappa=\hbar^2/(2mR^2)>0$. The operator in the Statement is
$\kappa(-i\partial_\phi-\alpha)^2$, so [F2] and [F3] give its periodic
domain, complete Fourier eigenbasis, energy list, and spectrum. If the flux
is shifted by $2\pi\hbar j/q$, then $\alpha$ shifts by $j$ and the unitary
multiplication $U_jf=e^{ij\phi}f$ intertwines the two Hamiltonians by [F3].
The same fact [F3] shows that a smooth single-valued periodic phase removing
$\alpha$ exists only for integral $\alpha$. Thus the spectrum and its gauge
periodicity follow conditionally from the declared ideal ring model; no
finite-width correction or measurement is asserted.

Use SI units with mass $m>0$ in kilograms, charge $q\in\mathbb R$ in
coulombs, action constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, vector-potential
components $A_j$ in tesla-metres, and scalar potential-energy function $V$ in
joules. For each integer $d\ge1$, let $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$
be real and let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ be bounded
below. Adopt the general-dimensional minimal-coupling assignment whose core
form is
$$q_{A,V}[u]=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\|(-i\hbar\partial_j-qA_j)u\|_2^2+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V|u|^2,\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C).$$
Use its closed form closure and the unique self-adjoint representing
Hamiltonian. For dimensional form norms use the fixed reference energy
$E_0=1\,\mathrm J$: apply the closed-form representation to
$q_{A,V}/E_0$ and multiply the representing operator by $E_0$.

The magnetic-field notation is dimension-specific. In $d=2$, with coordinates
$(x,y)$ and $A=(A_x,A_y)$, define the scalar perpendicular field
$$B_\perp(x,y)=\partial_xA_y(x,y)-\partial_yA_x(x,y),$$
in teslas. Thus $A=(0,Bx)$ gives $B_\perp=B$ for a constant signed scalar
$B$. In $d=3$, for coordinates $(x,y,z)$ and $A=(A_x,A_y,A_z)$, define the
field vector $\mathbf B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ in teslas by
$$\mathbf B=(\partial_yA_z-\partial_zA_y,\ \partial_zA_x-\partial_xA_z,\ \partial_xA_y-\partial_yA_x)=\nabla\times A.$$
No magnetic-field object is assigned by this notation in $d=1$.

For an optional spin-half degree of freedom in three dimensions, define
$$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_j=\frac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_j.$$
For a core spinor $u=(u_1,u_2)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^2)$,
define the spin-independent form
$$q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}[u_1]+q_{A,V}[u_2].$$
For a declared dimensionless real coupling $g$, adopt the effective Pauli core
form
$$q^{\mathrm P}_{A,V,g}[u]=q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]-\frac{gq}{2m}\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(x)^*(S\cdot\mathbf B(x))u(x)\,dx,$$
where $u^*$ is conjugate transpose and
$(S\cdot\mathbf B)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^3S_jB_j(x)$ for the three-dimensional
field vector just defined.
Include this term only in model instances where the resulting form is
closable and bounded below, and use its closed form closure and representing
Hamiltonian. No universal semiboundedness for arbitrary $A,V,g$ is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and let $d\ge1$ be an integer. Work in
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$\langle u,v\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u\overline v$, linear in the first
variable, using the quotient and complex-function conventions of the linked
Euclidean $L^2$ definitions. Fix real scalars $m>0$, $\hbar>0$, and $q$.
Let $A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be real and
let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ satisfy
$V\ge-v_0$ almost everywhere for some finite $v_0\ge0$. Put
$\mathscr D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and, for $u\in\mathscr D$,
define
$$\Pi_j^A u=-i\hbar\,\partial_j u-qA_j u\qquad (1\le j\le d).$$
For $u,v\in\mathscr D$ define the sesquilinear form
$$q_{A,V}(u,v)=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\langle\Pi_j^A u,\Pi_j^A v\rangle+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)u(x)\overline{v(x)}\,dx,$$
and write $q_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}(u,u)$. Each integral is finite: the test
functions and their magnetic derivatives are bounded with compact support,
and $V$ is integrable on compact sets. The form is Hermitian, densely
defined, and bounded below by $-v_0\|u\|_2^2$.

For $\varepsilon_0>0$ define its shifted form norm by
$$\|u\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}^2=q_{A,V}[u]+(v_0+\varepsilon_0)\|u\|_2^2.$$
The form is **closable** when every sequence $(u_n)\subset\mathscr D$ with
$\|u_n\|_2\to0$ and
$\|u_n-u_m\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$ as $n,m\to\infty$ also satisfies
$\|u_n\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$. This condition is independent of the
choice of $\varepsilon_0>0$. When it holds, the **closed form closure** is the
completion of $\mathscr D$ in this norm, identified with its $L^2$ limits;
the corresponding closed form is denoted $\overline q_{A,V}$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

formal coefficient as $g=2$. The conclusion is only the stated identity of
core differential expressions; the postulate separately requires a
closable semibounded form before assigning a self-adjoint Pauli Hamiltonian.
