Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice, and
the adopted spinless minimal-coupling form model. Let $m>0$ be mass in kilograms,
$q\ne0$ charge in coulombs, $B\ne0$ the constant signed perpendicular
field component in teslas, and $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. Let
$A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be $A(x,y)=(0,Bx)$ in tesla-metres; then
$B_\perp=\partial_xA_y-\partial_yA_x=B$ is its scalar perpendicular field.
Take wavefunctions in $L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$. Set $V=0$ and define the Hamiltonian by the
closed form of the core expression
$$q_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C).$$
The resulting Friedrichs Hamiltonian is unitarily equivalent, under partial
Fourier transformation in $y$ followed by
$x=\xi+\hbar k/(qB)$, to the constant family of oscillators
$$h(k)=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_\xi^2+\frac{(qB\xi)^2}{2m},\qquad k\in\mathbb R,$$
with its form-closed realization. Its spectrum is
$$\left\{\frac{\hbar|qB|}{m}\left(n+\frac12\right):n\in\mathbb N_0\right\}.$$
Every listed eigenvalue has infinite multiplicity, and every spectral measure
is purely atomic on this set; there is no continuous spectral measure. This is
a conditional model deduction, not a claim that a material realizes the
ideal infinite-plane Hamiltonian.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Adopt the static ring model of a spinless particle of mass $m>0$ kilograms
and charge $q\ne0$ coulombs constrained to a circle of radius $R>0$ metres.
Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, flux $\Phi$ in webers, and energies in joules.
The angular coordinate is $\phi\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$; the
single-valued wavefunction belongs to the periodic domain
$H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)$; the scalar potential is zero; and a static
tangential vector potential $A_\phi=\Phi/(2\pi R)$ has circulation
$\oint A\cdot d\ell=\Phi$, where $\Phi$ is flux in webers. Under the SI
minimal-coupling assignment, the Hamiltonian is
$$H_\Phi=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mR^2}\left(-i\partial_\phi-\alpha\right)^2,\qquad \alpha=\frac{q\Phi}{2\pi\hbar},$$
on that periodic domain. Its energies are
$$E_n(\Phi)=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mR^2}(n-\alpha)^2,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z,$$
with a complete periodic Fourier eigenbasis. For every $j\in\mathbb Z$,
$\Phi\mapsto\Phi+2\pi\hbar j/q$ gives a unitarily equivalent Hamiltonian;
a noninteger $\alpha$ cannot be removed by a single-valued periodic gauge
phase. These are conditional deductions of the ideal ring model.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. Let
$\kappa>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$. On
$H=L^2(S^1;\mathbb C)=L^2((0,2\pi),d\phi;\mathbb C)$ use the periodic domain
$H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)$ defined by periodic endpoint traces and define
$$T_\alpha f=\kappa(-i\partial_\phi-\alpha)^2f,\qquad D(T_\alpha)=H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1).$$
Then $T_\alpha$ is self-adjoint and the normalized characters
$e_n(\phi)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{in\phi}$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, form a complete
orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues $\lambda_n=\kappa(n-\alpha)^2$.
Its spectrum is the closed set $\{\lambda_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$ and its
spectral measures are purely atomic on that set. For every $j\in\mathbb Z$,
multiplication by $e^{ij\phi}$ unitarily intertwines $T_\alpha$ with
$T_{\alpha+j}$. A smooth periodic unit-modulus function $u$ satisfying
$u^{-1}(-i\partial_\phi-\alpha)u=-i\partial_\phi$ exists exactly when
$\alpha\in\mathbb Z$.

At $\alpha=1/2$, $E_n=\kappa(n-1/2)^2$. The nearest integers to $1/2$
are exactly $0$ and $1$, and both have squared distance $1/4$; every other
integer has distance at least $3/2$. Therefore $E_0=E_1=\kappa/4$ is the
ground energy and no other Fourier label attains it. The complete basis in
[F1] makes the ground eigenspace exactly two-dimensional, conditional on the ideal ring assumptions.

At $\alpha=0$, $E_n=\kappa n^2\ge0$, with equality exactly at the
integer $n=0$. The eigenbasis in [F1] then gives a one-dimensional ground
eigenspace, spanned by $e_0(\phi)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}$, again conditional on the ideal ring assumptions.
